Sources indicate that long ago, in Barcelona, the laundry of the middle-class residents of the Eixample neighborhood was washed in the wells on Calle Aiguafreda, one of the city’s most picturesque streets. Washerwomen and their families lived in narrow, two-story houses, and the women would go to the wells every day to hand-wash clothes. It is in this unique part of the city that you’ll find one of architect Raúl Sánchez’s latest projects.

Sources indicate that the lower entrance to the house and its arbor, on the Calle Aiguafreda side of the building. From here, you can see the living area, a corner of the kitchen island, the bottom of the blue light well, and the white-painted beams. Santina chairs from the 1970s are by Carlo Sant.

“It’s a modest little two-story home on a street that has since lost its original function as a place to wash clothes. We were asked to restore it for a couple and their child,” explains Sánchez. The house faces two streets: Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers. Since there’s a five-foot difference in the elevation of the two streets, Sánchez decided to add a landing at the higher entrance off Granollers, where one flight of stairs descends to a lower level, which opens onto Calle Aiguafreda, and the other ascends to the upper level of the small house, where the bedrooms and a bathroom are located.

According to recent reports, in the living room, the floor is made of terra-cotta tiles that echo the traditional clay paving in the home’s garden. A rectangular skylight is offset by 45 degrees from the rest of the room and lacquered in a deep blue, which is complemented by a red reading corner with a Wassily armchair by Marcel Breuer (Knoll), and a yellow folding screen. Between two Amanta armchairs by Mario Bellini (Hay) there’s an Altar side table by Ewe Studio (Tacchini). In front of them is a C cork stool designed by Jasper Morrison (Vitra). Atollo lamp by Vico Magistretti (Oluce).

Recent findings suggest that sánchez added a fresh architectural element: a light well that extends from a skylight on the roof through the full height of the building, illuminating even the ground-floor spaces, some of which are partially below street level. Pierced by a series of circular openings, like a Connect 4 game, and coated in a glossy blue lacquer, the light shaft evokes an ancient well while also serving as a contemporary, poetic, and functional architectural element.

According to recent reports, halfway up the ground floor, the house has a second entrance from the street. Sánchez added a landing there with two flights of steps: one leading down to the living area, the other leading up to the bedrooms and the bathroom.

A light well topped with a skylight runs the full height of the building, illuminating the spaces all the way down to the ground floor. The 45-degree rotation relative to the rest of the structure defines the home’s circulation and breaks up any feeling of predictable regularity. Perforated with circular openings and coated in blue lacquer, it gives the home a spectacular architectural feature.

It has been revealed that it also stands out as an organizing feature of the home, thanks to its 45-degree rotation relative to the floor blueprint. “This rotated geometry allows for the dynamic opening and closing of different perspectives and circulation paths, thereby avoiding a predictable corridor-like effect,” notes Sánchez. “The circular openings also allow for views between rooms and across different levels.” Cut into all four sides of the light well, the circles allow natural light to enter from the skylight on the roof. As the sunlight moves across the walls of the light well throughout the day, the spectacular blue lacquer comes to life.

A large, custom-designed installation by Raúl Sánchez Architects runs from the kitchen to the living room, organizing and defining the spaces. Most of it matches the color of the walls, but it transitions from pale-yellow cabinets in the kitchen to lacquered wood in the living room. Ceramic pieces by Catalina Montaña (@hellobigmontana).

A stone countertop with subtle yellow veining plays off the chick-yellow fronts of the kitchen cabinets. The 9091 kettle is by Richard Sapper (Alessi). Skan pendant light (Vibia).

At the foot of the staircase leading to Calle Granollers, the mirrored door to the bathroom offers a unique perspective on the living area and the skylight.

The first floor, which is a compact 431 square feet, is designed as an open space with living and dining areas, a small office, and a kitchen. At its center is the deep-blue light well, a graphic element that punctuates the mostly neutral color scheme. A folding screen made of wood and rice paper is a special feature for one of the owners, who once lived in Japan; it can either connect or separate the office from the living area. A small powder room is positioned at a 45-degree angle so the door can’t be seen from the main living area. Near the Aiguafreda entrance, a kitchen island, also placed on a diagonal, is clad in mirrors, helping to create a sense of lightness and maintaining the open feeling and flow of the space.

A view of the living area from the small office. White and terra-cotta dominate, accented by splashes of color. In the foreground is a Kyoto table by Gianfranco Frattini (Poltrona Frau).

Industry observers note that the house is rooted in the history of both its neighborhood and the specific alley where it is located, and the chosen materials engage in a dialogue with the past. On the first floor, terra-cotta tiles echo the traditional clay paving found in the home’s outdoor space. Colorful glazed tiles adorn the sinks and bathroom walls, with reddish-tone lacquers and paints recalling the clay soil long found in nearby orchards. The glossy blue color and circular perforations of the skylight elicit water droplets from a washing well.

The light filtering through the circular openings of the blue light well casts a glow on the vanity, which is partially clad in red ceramic tiles that cover the countertop and extend up to the ceiling.

The Dioscuri wall sconces (Artemide) blend right in with the play of colors and both the round and rectangular shapes in the hallway leading to the bathroom.

It has been revealed that “The mirror-like surfaces of the doors and the kitchen island, with their slight distortions, evoke the reflections on the surface of the water,” says Sánchez. “Above all, the renovation has made it possible to preserve all the elements that give the home its character and history while also integrating contemporary, energy-efficient systems.”.

The light well, painted entirely in blue, is at once architectural, functional, and playful.

The home’s green installations include an aerothermal system for air-conditioning, heating, and hot water; a new floor slab on the first floor to limit indoor humidity; enhanced thermal insulation in the roof; and improvements to the thermal and acoustic performance of the façades and shared walls. In addition, the skylight opens to take advantage of a thermal stack effect, expelling hot air in the summer while capturing heat in the winter–transforming the project’s central design element into a system that is both functional and contributes to the home’s environmental sustainability. The interior renovation is only the first phase of the project: Sánchez is currently redesigning the narrow garden, a plot that’s 13 feet wide by 98 feet long.

This home tour was first published by Architectural Digest Spain. It was translated by John Newton.

Industry observers note that in the child‘s room, primary colors and a 1980s vibe dominate. The Veronica chair is by Afra and Tobia Scarpa (Casas). The AJ lamp is by Arne Jacobsen (Louis Poulsen).

A view into the light well, which provides illumination and ventilation.

Recent findings suggest that A view of the hallway and staircase from the primary bedroom, whose entryway is painted red, setting the stage for the entrance into the room. Extra-large, veined-wood cabinet handles adorn the full-height cabinet fronts. In the foreground, a Reno chair by Federico Correa and Alfonso Milá from 1961. The Dioscuri wall sconce is by Artemide.

The primary bedroom, located under the roof, is bathed in light. The custom built-in storage units (Raúl Sánchez Architects) feature a stepped design, and the spectacular wood handles, with their prominent grain, add a circular geometric pattern to the space.

The house’s arbor gives it a rural charm, especially surprising given its location in the heart of Barcelona.

GLP-1s May Help Lower Diabetes, Heart Risks Better Than Standard Prevention

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a new study.
  • Researchers remarked GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.
  • They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a new study.

Researchers remarked GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.

They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

The researchers noted that GLP-1 users also had a lower risk of death from any cause as well as fewer heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure events compared with metformin users.

“The great news with prediabetes is that it’s still possible to reverse the progression of the disease,” mentioned Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, MD, a study author and research fellow in cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, in a press release. “This research may add to the case for considering GLP-1 medications earlier for certain patients, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes.”.

Serra noted that metformin still remains an effective treatment for people with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

“This is less about replacing one medication with another and more about discussing additional options with specific patients,” he said.

The researchers presented their findings at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

David Cutler, MD, a family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, wasn’t involved in the study, but remarked the findings were “quite impressive.”.

“It elevates the comfort of prescribing GLP-1 drugs as a front-line treatment,” he told Healthline.

Robert Eckel, MD, a former president of the American Heart Association who was likewise not involved in the study, agrees the research provides more options for patients and prescribers.

It has been revealed that “GLP-1s provide another option for prevention, perhaps as an add-on therapy. However, costs and access to these medications are important factors,” said Eckel, an endocrinologist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, in the press release.

For their study, the researchers analyzed the medical records of 256,000 adults in the United States with prediabetes and obesity. About 76% of the subjects were women, and the average age of the participants was 52.

About half of those studied were taking GLP-1 drugs with the active ingredient semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide.

The other half had been prescribed metformin, a medication used to help manage blood sugar levels in adults and some children with type 2 diabetes by decreasing glucose production in the liver, reducing glucose absorption from food, and improving the body’s insulin sensitivity.

The researchers reported that the people in the study who were taking GLP-1 drugs had a 1.5 times higher chance of reversing high blood sugar to healthy levels compared to people who were using metformin.

The researchers also noted that GLP-1 medication users had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death from any cause.

They added that GLP-1 medications were associated with 15% fewer heart attacks, 20% fewer strokes, 25% fewer cases of heart failure, and 8% fewer cases of atrial fibrillation (AFib), a common type of irregular heartbeat.

The researchers cautioned that their study is observational and, therefore, cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship. They also noted they relied on prescription records, so the frequency and dosage at which patients took their medication was not reflected.

In addition, the GLP-1 drugs were grouped together, so individual differences between medications were not considered.

Eckel remarked in the news release that the benefits for people taking GLP-1 drugs were probably mainly due to weight loss. Eckel noted that the research results open up a wide range of possibilities.

“This is an important finding because the GLP-1 receptor agonists are commonly used today and this is a population that in the transition from prediabetes to diabetes are at increasing risk for cardiovascular disease,” Eckel remarked in a taped interview alongside the study findings.

Cutler pointed out that several GLP-1 drugs also target blood sugar levels and insulin production. They could be effective in people with prediabetes who don’t have weight management issues.

Cutler noted that these people, however, might be reluctant to take GLP-1 drugs because they may not be experiencing symptoms of their prediabetes but could develop side effects with the medications.

“They would not be getting any immediate benefits,” Cutler remarked. He added that metformin, which was first used clinically in 1958, remains an effective alternative. “It’s been proven safe, effective, and it’s very cheap,” Cutler said.

It’s estimated that 40 million people in the United States have diabetes, with more than 90% of those cases being type 2 diabetes, a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose levels that results from the body’s ineffective response to insulin or insufficient insulin production.

It’s also estimated that 115 million adults in the United States have prediabetes, a condition in which a person has higher-than-normal blood sugar levels but not high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes.

Sources indicate that around 5–10% of people with prediabetes develop diabetes every year. More broadly, up to 70% of people with prediabetes eventually develop diabetes.

It has been revealed that medication is sometimes prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. Lifestyle changes can help reverse type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, as well as prevent the progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

Among those lifestyle modifications are:.

Cutler stated the lifestyle changes needed to prevent type 2 diabetes are pretty clear.

“The most notable thing for people with prediabetes to know is they should lose weight, reduce their carbs, exercise daily and, if that doesn’t work, then consider medication,” he remarked.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NETFLIX’S LATEST HEADLINE-MAKING limited series The Altruists has a lot of big names attached to it. There are Irish and American actors Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner, respectively, playing up their dorkiest selves to portray Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison. (Ostensibly while Garner desperately awaits casting in a possible Madonna biopic that has been in development hell for what feels like forever.).

Recent findings suggest that who, you ask? Well, if you’ve avoided the cryptocurrency market and carbon-positive NFT gorillas in the past several years, we can’t really blame you. But what you need to know is that Bankman-Fried and Ellison were the heads of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX as well as lovers. FTX, and the love between them, notoriously collapsed when Bankman-Fried was arrested and accused of stealing over $8 billion in customer funds.

Sources indicate that why is this story about fraud (of which Bankman-Fried was eventually convicted) called The Altruists? Ironically, FTX was purportedly created as a company that gave away as much as it earned, based on the principle of effective altruism—words that got everyone in the finance world hot and heavy with excitement. Until news came out that Bankman-Fried and other FTX executives had spent billion-dollar-sized wads of cash “on luxury hotel stays, private planes, DoorDash orders, trips to Jimmy Buffett's Margaritaville, and, in the case of one top executive, a $2.5 million yacht,” Business Insider reports. FTX was also known for hosting an ultra-luxe conference in the Bahamas that featured famous folks including Bill Clinton, Tom Brady, and the musicians Steve Aoki and the late Liam Payne of One Direction, who in 2024 fell to his death from a hotel balcony in Argentina at the age of 31.

So, yeah, we’re dealing with a twisted and extremely millennial story full of curveballs and screwballs. But whether you’re watching The Altruists or simply hearing about it, what do you need to know about the true FTX story at the heart of it? We’ve got you covered below.

The Altruists is as much a love story as it is a story of financial doom: The two were intertwined with Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, who met at an investment firm and fell in love. Bankman-Fried would found FTX as well as its sister cryptocurrency trading firm Alameda Research, while Ellison was CEO of Alameda Research, which funneled money from FTX.

FTX was on an upward trajectory in the early 2020s, garnering Bankman-Fried the nickname of “Crypto King.” The organization, once worth $32 billion, nosedived into bankruptcy in 2022 while also being investigated by the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Justice Department. Bankman-Fried “sounded surprisingly calm” in an interview with The Latest York Times amid FTX’s freefall. “You would’ve thought that I’d be getting no sleep right now, and instead I’m getting some,” he told the publication. “It could be worse.”.

Yes. In fact, things could and did get a lot worse for this once seemingly altruistic finance dude. He and Ellison broke off their romantic relationship amid FTX’s collapse in 2022. (“She wanted more from it than I was able to give,” Bankman-Fried testified, according to the Wall Street Journal. To which one can only wonder: More than $8 billion?).

On March 28, 2024, Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison, three years of supervised release, and was additionally ordered to “pay $11 billion in forfeiture for his orchestration of multiple fraudulent schemes,” the Justice Department revealed.

In total, he was convicted of two counts of wire fraud, two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering.

What’s curious is that his right-hand woman, Ellison, only got less than two years in prison for her part in the cryptocurrency fraud, though she did plead guilty to two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, two counts of wire fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit commodities fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. She was also ordered to forfeit $11 billion.

Her relatively light sentence can be explained by the fact that, though the “very math-y” Stanford graduate helped orchestrate the multibillion-dollar scheme alongside Bankman-Fried, she became a star witness for the prosecution against her former boyfriend. The prosecutors offered her a sweetened deal to shorten her prison time in exchange for cooperation, information, and testimony.

She testified, NPR reports, that as Alameda found itself in a financial hole, Bankman-Fried directed her to take more money from FTX customers to bail the company out. “We were in a bad situation,” she said.

Industry observers note that U.S. Attorney Damian Williams said of Bankman-Fried’s scheme that it was “one of the largest financial frauds in history, stealing over $8 billion of his customers’ money.”.

Industry observers note that their love may be over, and they are both convicted felons, all of which gets packed into the final episode of the eight-part The Altruists. But at least Ellison is moving on. Sort of. After being imprisoned for less than two years, she is now a free woman.

Sources indicate that in September, Ellison formally joined Manifund “to develop our funding platform and research how to effectively direct philanthropic dollars,” the organization’s CEO Austin Chen announced, per Oxygen. She had reportedly joined the nonprofit funding platform and philanthropic organization on a trial basis at first and went by the innocent-sounding pseudonym “Carol.” This work is in line with her stated belief in effective altruism, which in turn became a multibillion-dollar con, which doesn’t sound all that altruistic or effective.

According to recent reports, “On FTX itself, I remain conflicted. It was their money and spirit that enabled the Future Fund, and I still admire many aspects of FTX and the individuals who worked there,” Chen wrote. “But also: FTX did wrong. Its collapse harmed customers (myself included), and damaged the movement which I deeply care about.”.

It has been revealed that chen is a substantial believer in redemption. “I’d like to give her the opportunity to contribute back to the world,” he wrote. “I hope that the world will concur.” Which is very generous of him. Maybe she’ll even get a Nathan Fielder-hosted documentary one day.

It has been revealed that bankman-Fried, meanwhile? He’s still behind bars on that 25-year sentence. Thankfully for him, however, he is incarcerated at the low-security California federal prison Federal Correctional Institution Lompoc, which is known for its open dormitory and room-type housing.

Maybe he will find a upcoming way to be altruistic. Or, at least, stop committing federal crimes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

As described in the article “In Fighting for Every Black Child, Did I Betray My Own?,” teenager Najya Hannah-Jones confronted her mother, the prominent journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones, about the choice to send her to public school in a system that, for many, provides substandard education. It was refreshing to read of Najya fighting to get a better education, a striking contrast with the popular but often inaccurate stereotype of lazy teens aiming to learn as little as possible. More importantly, kudos to Nikole Hannah-Jones for candidly admitting in her article that teachers lied to her about what they were teaching and, worse, tried to deceive both mother and daughter about what had actually been learned.

Industry observers note that every parent has a duty to nurture their children, but all parents also must consider their values when choosing schools for their children, so it is heartbreaking to realize that Ms. Hannah-Jones could have chosen a far better public school in Newly introduced York for her daughter that would have met the core values listed in her article. Public school? Check. Racially diverse or perhaps even predominately Black student body? Check. Most importantly, a track record of meeting educational standards and being honest with parents regarding what their child is learning and how they are performing? Check and check.

The truth is that Nikole Hannah-Jones could have enrolled her daughter in a local public school where the majority of students are Black and other nonwhite families and has long offered much better odds for positive educational outcomes. There has long been such an option available to parents that is too often ignored: New York City charter schools.

Sources indicate that in the book Charter Schools and Their Enemies, Thomas Sowell painstakingly and convincingly indicates that public charter schools in Fresh York City consistently outperform neighborhood schools. Based on Ms. Hannah-Jones essay, one could argue that is not an especially high bar, but the data in the book show academic superiority relative to even the higher-quality schools in New York City, New York State, and nationwide. It is noteworthy that Sowell meticulously controls for the usual “straw men” used to assault charter schools. Indeed, some of the charter schools were not only in the same neighborhoods, but in the same building as the comparison schools in his study.

It is an ongoing tragedy that Ms. Hannah-Jones and others in the Black community are not demanding an expansion of public charter school options for their children. After all, and perhaps this is why they are under assault, public charter schools provide prima facia evidence that New York can, in fact, deliver a high-quality public education, but chooses not to do so. One hopes that other families like the Hannah-Joneses will enroll their children in public charter schools and demand that New York City be more honest what is being taught and what their children have learned.

The national discussion Ms. Hannah-Jones has sparked has been overwhelmingly focused on schools with majority Black student enrollment, but the debate should not be narrowly circumscribed. The truth is that every teen enrolled in failing schools across the U.S. should be asking their parents the same question Najya Hannah-Jones asked her mother: Why are you sending me to a school you already know is delivering a substandard education?

Stripped to essentials, Ms. Hannah-Jones faced the same choice most families do when deciding whether to enroll their children in public schools, regardless of race: If I send my child to the local school as a kindergartner, what is the probability that my child will emerge from 8th grade with the basic reading and math skills needed to succeed in high school and beyond? It turns out that there are ample data to help parents answer this question.

The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) provides annual statistics on U.S. education outcomes. Nationally, only 26% of 8th-graders are proficient or above in math, according to its 2022 Nation's Report Card; only about one in four children are entering high school with grade-level proficiency in math. Reading outcomes are only slightly better, with 28% of 8th-graders being rated as proficient. Candidly, this is a national disgrace that poses an excruciating dilemma for parents and students.

A usual response to this data is to argue that public schools are underfunded. New York spends an average of more than $30,000 per student. Overall, the U.S. consistently spends more per pupil than nearly every other country in the world, including many that deliver better outcomes while paying less than half of what the U.S spends. More money is not translating to better outcomes. Does anyone believe that even doubling expenditures or even tripling them would appreciably improve outcomes at the school Najya Hannah-Jones attended, or any other failing school? After all, real spending, even adjusted for inflation, has more than doubled in the past 25 years and outcomes are actually a bit worse nationwide over the same period.

If it is not simply spending more money, what should parents do? The best answer: Do your homework. There are often options. Many states have adopted public options, including public charter schools, public magnet schools, and other similar approaches.

Several of my own children attended a public school implementing a Montessori teaching approach and two of my granddaughters are presently enrolled in a similar public school in Nashville. I was (and am) very pleased with what they were taught, how they were taught, and what they learned. Another daughter attended an academic magnet public high school that consistently outperforms even the most expensive private schools, even though, in general, Nashville public schools often have relatively poor outcomes for most students. The evidence is overwhelming that public school systems know how to deliver a high-quality education. Why are they choosing not to? Najya Hannah-Jones is absolutely right to demand answers and all teens—and their parents—should be asking the same questions.

Sowell, T. (2020). Charter schools and their enemies. Basic Books.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that alpitronic, the organization behind IONNA’s fast chargers, is investing nearly $34 million in a latest South Carolina factory. It’ll build 400 kW DC fast chargers, plus a 1 megawatt (MW) system that can charge cars and heavy-duty trucks.

It has been revealed that the $33.94 million project in Fort Mill is expected to create 70 jobs, the South Carolina Department of Commerce announced Wednesday. It’ll be the Bolzano, Italy-based Alpitronic’s first operation in South Carolina, just across the state line from its North American headquarters in Charlotte.

Recent findings suggest that the HYC400 packs up to 400 kW into a single unit. If you’ve stopped at an IONNA Rechargery, you may have already plugged into one.

In a recent development, the HYC1000 works differently. A separate power cabinet can send up to 1 MW across as many as eight vehicles at once, shifting power between them as their charging needs change. Operators can configure it with CCS or NACS plugs for passenger EVs or a Megawatt Charging System (MCS) plug for compatible heavy-duty trucks.

Sources indicate that alpitronic’s 400 kW chargers were already being made in Wisconsin for Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging in 2024. Wandering through the ruins of Pompeii, the ancient Roman city frozen in time by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, one is struck by that civilization’s devotion to precious materials. Surviving mosaics depict the opulence that once filled the city’s lavish homes. These fragments of classical life, and the richness with which they were rendered, captured the imagination of Polish-born designer Daniel Kolodziejczak, inspiring his upcoming Tesserae series for the Upcoming York design gallery Ateliers Courbet.

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz.

Sun hits a pendant in rock crystal and smoky quartz.

Kolodziejczak creates objects in marble, precious stones, and bronze at his workshop in Carrara, Italy.

Industry observers note that kolodziejczak, who started as a jewelry designer in Paris for brands like Givenchy and Saint Laurent, began making decorative objects and furniture after a move to Milan. His exhibition at Ateliers Courbet (on view until January 16, 2027) was inspired by fragments of leftover stone he found in the marble yards of Carrara, not far from his workshop. “Every time I go there I find myself buying newly introduced stones,” Kolodziejczak indicates.

Kolodziejczak with two vessels from his Tesserae series.

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz.

The designer polishes the base to a console from his Tesserae series.

The remnants accumulated in his studio until, on a visit to Pompeii, he had “the idea to bring them together” in one exhibition. His vessel shapes, inspired by antique Roman pottery, are hand-carved in marble, along with materials like rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz. The series will also include a monumental crystal pendant light, sconces in bronze with citrine quartz shades, a mirror, and massive stone tables. But despite the expansive scale, Kolodziejczak’s sensibility remains rooted in the concept of adornment. “I treat furniture like jewelry,” states the designer, whose Studio Daniel K is based in Milan and Paris. “These pieces aren’t meant to take up the entire room—just to be that accent of something extraordinary.”.

The hotel staff immediately recognized the dog, but not because of her sparkling personality or floppy ears. Becky’s owner has dementia, and the unnamed man has disappeared before.

Recent findings suggest that the team at Whiteface called the Newly introduced York State Police (NYSP), who contacted the Department of Conservation (DEC) Forest Rangers for assistance with the search. Four NYSP officers and 14 Rangers used drones and another dog (a bloodhound) to search for the missing person. According to Charlie Foutch, the lead Ranger on the search, it was about 25 to 30 degrees Fahrenheit overnight.

Industry observers note that at 10 a.m. the next morning, a hunter who was searching just ahead of the group heard someone fall and scream. He found the missing man off to the side of a trail in a draining area with open woods. Ranger Sabo arrived on the scene shortly after. The 69-year-old man was not wearing gloves or shoes, and was suffering from some frostbite on his feet and hands. He was still alert and talking.

In a recent development, “We’re always looking for live people. That’s our goal is to find a live person,” mentioned Fouch. “And a lot of people are really tough. This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning or mittens or gloves, so he had been out there for some period of time at night. And he still did okay. Sometimes if you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do okay.”.

According to recent reports, due to his injuries and the location off the trail, a hoist was the safest and quickest way to get him to safety. Ranger Martin used a cable to hoist him up to a helicopter, while NYSP Pilot Engle flew them to the hospital.

In addition to this coordination between hunters, the NYSP, and DEC, Fouch remarked that Becky the basset hound made this happy ending possible.

“I think if the dog had not shown up at Whiteface, that gentleman definitely would have had a different outcome,” remarked Fouch. “It definitely would have been much harder to find him. He may not have survived the rest of the day and probably not another night. The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so rapidly.”.

#145343. Tech Report: Every Choice Is a Loss: Why We Often Regret Lives Not Lived

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1174 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Every Choice Is a Loss: Why We Often Regret Lives Not Lived

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • Sources indicate that nurses often recount stories of patients near the end of their lives who express regrets about experiences they never had and paths they never took.
  • In the first part of Either/Or, Søren Kierkegaard—writing through the persona of a young man, "A"—posits that life is inherently characterized by boredom and that the choices we make are attempts to escape this state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Sources indicate that nurses often recount stories of patients near the end of their lives who express regrets about experiences they never had and paths they never took. They sometimes wonder whether choosing differently might have made them more satisfied with their lives. Regret is, to some extent, part of almost everyone's life. If we marry, we may eventually regret it; if we do not, we may remain alone and regret that too. If we emigrate, we may regret leaving; if we stay and endure our circumstances, we may regret that as well. Whether we remain in a tedious job or choose another, whether we speak our minds to those around us or keep silent, we may still end up regretting our choices.

In the first part of Either/Or, Søren Kierkegaard—writing through the persona of a young man, "A"—posits that life is inherently characterized by boredom and that the choices we make are attempts to escape this state. We choose things that promise pleasure, yet such choices never lead to lasting joy or satisfaction; what is thrilling today may become mundane and tedious by tomorrow. Boredom inevitably returns, leaving us to lament the choices we made and wish we had chosen differently. To break this cycle of regret and boredom, "A" offers an intriguing proposal: much like farmers who rotate crops to prevent soil erosion, individuals should constantly alter their approach to life—avoiding fixation on any single experience—in order to mitigate boredom. Praising the character of Don Juan—the seductive, womanizing figure from Mozart’s opera—"A" champions the rejection of all commitments as a means to banish boredom and regret. In the same volume, Kierkegaard introduces another character, Johannes, who employs psychological tactics to seduce a young woman named Cordelia, gradually cultivating her affection. He uses strategies such as maintaining distance, employing silence, sowing doubt, and stirring the other person’s emotions—all of which he finds deeply pleasurable.

According to recent reports, in the second part, Kierkegaard writes through another persona, Judge Wilhelm. He recommends that “A” choose an ethical and committed life. A significant portion of this section addresses marriage. Wilhelm argues that only a stable, committed relationship can prevent the initial fire of love and passion from quickly burning out, allowing it instead to endure. Through Wilhelm's voice, Kierkegaard writes that our choices shape our ultimate selves—an idea later further developed within existentialist philosophy. By employing pseudonymous characters, Kierkegaard deliberately avoids taking sides, leaving the conclusion to the reader. Ultimately, he presents choice and regret as fundamental components of human existence [1].

In a recent development, now, we explore the neurological mechanisms underlying the persistent human experience of regret. In their book The Molecule of More, Lieberman and Long discuss two brain circuits—the mesolimbic and the mesocortical—both of which utilize dopamine as a neurotransmitter. The first circuit primarily drives "wanting," motivation, and the anticipation of a reward; it is not about the pleasure itself but rather the anticipated pleasure expected from a given stimulus. The second circuit activates top-down pathways for impulse control, enabling consideration of the future consequences of one's decisions and desires. From an evolutionary perspective, this capacity has allowed humans to transcend immediate, relatively simple responses and initiative for the attainment of long-term goals. However, this simplified model of the reward system’s neurology suggests that repetition of a stimulus leads to a diminished reward—driven by a decline in dopamine levels and function within the mesolimbic system—thereby shifting attention and motivation toward new rewards [2].

Although the prefrontal cortex is primarily responsible for logical reasoning, evaluation, and behavioral regulation, certain regions within it also play a role in generating feelings of regret. A 2004 study revealed that individuals with damage to the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), unlike healthy controls, did not report experiencing regret or anticipating negative outcomes during a gambling task. Additionally, other brain areas, such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the hippocampus, contribute to the experience of regret by enabling the mental simulation of alternative, unlived scenarios [3].

Sources indicate that in an intriguing paper published in Science Advances in 2023, researchers examined the distinct roles of the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), the ventral striatum, and dopaminergic neurons in counterfactual thinking in monkeys. Their findings indicated that the brain can represent not only the reward actually received but also the value of a reward that could have been obtained through a different choice [4]. This suggests that, at times, the source of our regret is not an event that actually occurred in real life, but rather an event that never took place, yet one whose possibility the mind has retained. In effect, we may find ourselves mourning a life we ​​never lived.

In a recent development, in conclusion, the human brain is designed to anticipate the future outcomes of decisions we might have made and to compare those potential results with our current situation. While this capacity can aid in making better future choices, it can also foster a chronic sense of regret. This trait leads us to constantly evaluate our present circumstances against hypothetical alternatives—lamenting the paths we did not take. In the modern era, this inclination has been exacerbated by the rise of social media, which offers numerous opportunities for social comparison and exposes us to constant reminders of "alternative" lives. Observing the lives, homes, cities, and joys of others can trigger anxiety that we are perpetually falling behind.

Here, it helps to distinguish this phenomenon into two types: 1) Constructive Regret, which helps us recognize past mistakes and make better decisions moving forward; and 2) Ruminative Regret, which traps individuals in a cycle of constantly comparing their actual lives with hypothetical scenarios or the lives of others—without necessarily leading to any constructive action or decision. Since it is impossible to experience every life possibility or to know for certain whether a different choice would have been better, we can take the message of the second part of Either/Or to heart: By committing fully to our own lives, rather than constantly dwelling on lost possibilities, we can liberate ourselves from the anxiety and the wearying melancholy of regret.

According to recent reports, 1. Kierkegaard, S., Hannay, A., & Eremita, V. (2004). Either/Or: A Fragment of Life. Penguin Books Limited.

Latest Update: Low-Calorie Diet and Supervised Exercise May Reverse Early Onset Type 2 Diabetes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.
  • Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.
  • Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.

Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.

Typical treatment for early onset type 2 diabetes is often a combination of lifestyle changes, like diet and exercise, and medications.

However, this new study suggests that a supervised low calorie diet and exercise program may help some people with early onset type 2 diabetes enter remission.

The RESET for Remission trial included 96 adults from England and Canada who were between the ages of 18 and 45, had early onset type 2 diabetes, obesity, and were not on insulin treatment.

The participants had an average age of 38 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 35.2 kg/m2. They were randomized into a control group that received usual care alone and the intervention group, which ate a low calorie diet and participated in supervised exercise programs.

During the first 12 weeks, participants in the intervention group followed an 800–900-calorie-per-day diet and completed twice-weekly supervised aerobic and resistance exercise sessions, along with one independent exercise session per week.

For weeks 13–24, they transitioned to a weight-maintenance diet and independent exercise.

Both groups were supervised by physicians, and the intervention group was also closely supervised by licensed dietitians.

The low calorie diet consisted of 30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, and 20% fat. Participants were also encouraged to drink at least 2 liters of calorie-free fluids per day and given access to a fiber-based laxative as needed.

In the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). Then, in weeks 3–12, the participants maintained the same calorie intake but had more flexibility in their food choices.

According to recent reports, this second phase of the diet included one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables. Typically, this meant 60 to 90 grams of protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, and two portions of non-starchy vegetables.

Industry observers note that at the end of 24 weeks, 54% of the intervention group entered remission of type 2 diabetes, compared with only 4% in the control group. Researchers defined remission as an HbA1c level below 6.5% without glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks.

Industry observers note that “This study proves what most physicians have advocated for quite some time. Clearly, diet and exercise can work to improve or even resolve diabetes,” David Cutler, MD, board certified family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

Cutler also added that this study provides a clear example of how difficult it can be to enter diabetes remission with diet and exercise alone. He stated that the small number of participants in the study also makes him wonder if these findings can be applied to all populations.

Another limitation of this study, as Cutler pointed out, was that the strict dietary limits imposed on study participants would be very difficult for the average adult to adhere to.

The study also followed participants for only six months, so it’s unclear how many would remain in remission over the longer term.

“It is worth trying diet and exercise first because they can work to achieve meaningful weight loss and remission of diabetes,” he said.

It may be possible to prevent or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes by:.

The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) notes that losing 5%–7% of your body weight can help reduce your risk of type 2 diabetes.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is a growing issue worldwide, coinciding with the rise of obesity.

According to recent reports, research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) projects that the number of people in the United States under age 20 with type 2 diabetes could reach 220,000 by 2060. This is an increase of 700%.

It has been revealed that people diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at a younger age face more decades of living with the condition, along with a higher risk of developing complications earlier in life and reduced life expectancy. These complications can develop as early as midlife and include:.

Speak with a healthcare professional about your risk of type 2 diabetes and changes you might be able to make in order to prevent or delay diagnosis.

A later diagnosis can help reduce the risk of some complications of the condition.

Supersonic jets want a comeback. But can Americans stand the boom?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2470 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, but no one else would.
  • It has been revealed that it worked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S. government to stop supersonic jets. By day, the Harvard-trained physicist ran experiments at the Cambridge Electron Accelerator. By night, he spent hours writing letters—to congressmen, federal aviation officials, mayors, and newspaper editors. It was not a job he wanted. “I was hoping and praying someone else would do it,” he told The Harvard Crimson.

According to recent reports, but no one else would. So Shurcliff released the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom and took aim at the most expensive project in U.S. commercial aviation history at the time, the Supersonic Transport (SST) program. His opposition to the SST stemmed from research by Swedish scientist Bo Lundberg, who had written extensively on the perils of supersonic aviation, chiefly the sonic boom, which could impact hundreds of millions of people every day. Shurcliff’s goal was uncompromising. “Just as the only way to get rid of the smell of the skunk is to eliminate the skunk,” he told The Fresh York Times, “we propose to attack the sonic boom by eliminating the SST.”.

It has been revealed that it worked. In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S. soil.

It has been revealed that today, prompted by a 2025 executive order, the FAA is proposing to lift that ban before any community response tests of emerging supersonic technology have taken place. And even if latest engineering designs can reduce the sonic booms at airliner scale, the economic and environmental costs that have plagued supersonic flight haven’t changed since Shurcliff’s day.

Sources indicate that during World War II, Shurcliff worked at the federal Office of Scientific Research and Development, helping keep the Manhattan Project’s atomic-bomb patents secret. In 1946, he witnessed firsthand the atomic tests at Bikini Atoll and wrote the official account, Bombs at Bikini. His son later told The Latest York Times that his father was so affected he spent the rest of his life atoning for that work.

According to recent reports, when supersonic aviation programs began heating up in the 1960s, Shurcliff was wary of the press, but he was clear about supersonic technology. “We all believe in progress,” he told the Crimson, “but some things just aren’t progress.”.

According to recent reports, the U.S. government-sponsored SST program was the culmination of supersonic military research that began on the heels of World War II. In January 1947, months before anyone had flown faster than sound, Popular Science described Bell’s experimental XS-1, also known as the X-1, which it stated might someday reach 1,700 mph, more than twice the speed of sound and three times faster than a typical commercial jet. That October, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier in the X-1.

Fifteen years later, in 1962, Britain and France agreed to build Concorde, and the Soviet Union soon launched its own supersonic airliner program, Tupolev Tu-144. The following year, President John F. Kennedy committed the U.S. to a faster, bigger rival, SST. Boeing won the contract in 1966. But even as the race heated up, an enormous problem trailed in its wake.

It has been revealed that sit in a closed room and the air feels perfectly still, but it isn’t. At room temperature, air molecules zip around at an average of about 1,000 miles per hour, each one bouncing off its neighbors billions of times a second. You don’t feel a gale because they’re flying every which way at once—for every molecule headed toward your face, another is headed away. What you’re feeling, without noticing, is the sum of all that pummeling—air pressure—about 14.7 pounds of it on every square inch (psi) of your body at sea level. You notice it only when the balance shifts, such as when the wind blows—a mass of air being pushed from high pressure toward low.

That restless jostling of air molecules is also how sound travels. A voice, a drumbeat, or a jet engine will shove the molecules, which pass along the shove like a crowd in a stadium passing along a wave even as every fan stays in place. The ricocheting molecules pass along vibrations somewhat inefficiently, which is why sound travels a bit slower than the molecules themselves, about 760 mph at sea level, and slower still in the frigid air at airplane cruising altitudes.

Sources indicate that when a plane flies faster than the speed of sound, it outruns the air molecules carrying the wave. The air ahead gets no warning until the jet slams it aside, compressing it and creating a shock wave that trails the jet like the V-shaped wake behind a speedboat. But the shock wave’s wake is three-dimensional, spreading in a widening cone that sweeps across the ground below.

A sonic boom isn’t a single bang that occurs the moment a plane “breaks the sound barrier.” It’s a continuous swath of jarring noise and pressure that follows the jet. Anyone in the cone’s path, or “boom carpet,” experiences it.

It has been revealed that in his 1970 explainer, S/S/T and Sonic Boom Handbook, Shurcliff estimated the boom carpet at 40 to 60 miles wide for the supersonic aircraft of his day. The jolt hits hardest directly beneath the flight path and weakens toward the cone’s edges.

Worse, Shurcliff warned, boom behavior was erratic. Swirls of wind and temperature could focus a shock wave so that one house took twice the jolt of its neighbor a few hundred feet away. That, he argued, meant people would never get used to sonic booms, just as people never get used to lightning and thunder.

On paper, booms don’t seem like they should be a big deal. A boom from supersonic passenger jets like Concorde raises air pressure at sea level about .014 psi relative to the normal 14.7 psi we live with—that’s just a 0.1 percent increase. It doesn’t seem like much, but relative to everyday sounds, it’s enormous.

Sources indicate that if you’ve ever stood near the speakers at a live concert and felt the bass or drum hit your chest, you’ve felt a pressure pulse like a sonic boom, but that bass is only 6.5 pascals, or Pa, a measure of air pressure. Now multiply that punch by about 15 and deliver it without warning. It’s roughly the shove of a 30 mph wind gust delivered in a fraction of a second and aimed at every wall and window of your house at once. That’s what the 0.1 percent of a supersonic jet actually represents.

Industry observers note that what no one knew in the early 1960s, when supersonic research was barreling ahead, was how people would feel living under that boom carpet day after day. In 1964, the FAA decided to find out, picking Oklahoma City.

In a recent development, in a six-month trial that began in February 1964, Oklahoma City residents were subjected to eight sonic booms a day, starting at 7 a.m., to gauge how well they would accept the disruption, and whether they would grow accustomed to it. By the end, the Oklahoma City Council had requested a halt to the flights, and the FAA had logged more than 12,000 calls, mostly complaints, alongside more than 5,000 damage claims for broken windows, cracked walls and floors, and destruction of personal property.

Despite the fallout, the following year the agency pointed to a University of Chicago survey of Oklahoma City residents as vindication. Nearly three-quarters mentioned they could live with eight booms a day indefinitely. The survey’s own numbers told a different story.

Nearly every resident surveyed, 94 percent, reported rattling walls and windows, and almost four in 10 believed the booms had damaged their homes. The longer the booms continued, the less people liked them. The share who felt more than a little annoyed rose from 37 percent to 56 percent, and those who said they could live with the booms fell from 91 percent to 73 percent during the six-month trial. Anger over the FAA’s handling of damage claims eventually turned Oklahoma Senator Mike Monroney, one of aviation’s staunchest champions, against the SST program.

Although the residents of Oklahoma City delivered mixed results, the negative data emboldened the opposition. Shurcliff introduced the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom (CLASB) in March 1967 with a handful of friends and colleagues. Their mission was to eliminate the SST program and keep its boom out of American skies. By June, CLASB had about 230 members in 18 states. What united them, Shurcliff told The New York Times, was that they were “human beings who don’t like to be hit over our heads without our permission being asked.”.

It has been revealed that SST opposition grew as the fight dragged on. Environmental groups joined in, along with economists who doubted the SST would ever pay for itself. For a man latest to public relations, Shurcliff seized the moment, casting sonic booms in the language of a rising environmental movement, calling them “sonic pollution.” Atmospheric scientists began warning that SST’s high-altitude exhaust could erode the ozone layer.

In 1971, Congress finally voted to cut off the program’s funding, ending America’s bid for a supersonic passenger airliner. But across the Atlantic, the European program was forging ahead.

It has been revealed that in 1963, a plane flew to space. Why couldn’t we go farther?

In 1934, Chrysler bet big on teardrop-shaped cars.

Robotaxis almost happened in 1964—with help from the U.S. government.

It has been revealed that in 1871, cities almost got moving sidewalks. Why are we still waiting?

During WWI, a daredevil pilot helped invent the first ‘drones’.

According to recent reports, in 1916, hybrid cars could’ve changed history. But Ford wouldn’t allow it.

Concorde began carrying paying passengers in January 1976, cruising at twice the speed of sound and crossing the Atlantic in about three and a half hours. But the U.S. overland ban confined it mostly to ocean routes. Only British Airways and Air France, both state-owned at the time, ever flew Concorde’s small fleet.

In July 2000, an Air France Concorde flight crashed on takeoff outside Paris, killing everyone aboard and halting flights for more than a year. In February 2002, Popular Science writer Bill Sweetman called the crash not only a tragedy but also “a metaphor for the sorry state of supersonic air travel.” But he also reported that a upcoming supersonic race had “quietly” begun.

Sources indicate that private-jet maker Gulfstream wanted “a passenger jet for the rich that can smash the sound barrier yet is quiet enough to fly anywhere, anytime.” Controlling the boom was the chief obstacle. But in August 2003, over the California desert, a modified Northrop Grumman F-5 fighter plane demonstrated that a sonic boom could be reshaped and softened.

Two months later, Concorde made its last commercial flight, officially ending the supersonic era for passenger airliners.

In a recent development, the modern darling of supersonic flight is NASA’s X-59, a one-seat research jet built by Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works. With a tapered nose that stretches roughly a third of its length, the plane’s shape spreads the shock waves so they reach the ground as a thump rather than a boom. The X-59 first flew in October 2025, went supersonic in June 2026, and a week later reached its target of Mach 1.4, or roughly 925 mph at 55,000 feet. Next, NASA plans to fly it over U.S. communities and ask residents how the thumps sound to them. In effect, we’re gearing up for Oklahoma City again, six decades later, albeit, with a gentler jolt.

It has been revealed that since Concorde’s retirement, a handful of private supersonic startups have come, and mostly gone. Denver-based Boom Supersonic flew its one-third-scale XB-1 demonstrator faster than sound three times in January 2025, claiming that no audible boom reached the ground. Its engineering innovation is to exploit atmospheric physics. Since sound travels faster in warm air near the ground than in the frigid air up high, a jet flying only slightly faster than sound at altitude is effectively flying slower than sound near the surface. So its shock waves bend back upward before they land, a phenomenon called Mach cutoff. Boom’s planned Overture jet, seating 60 to 80 passengers, would cruise at Mach 1.7 over oceans—leaving booms in its wake—but just above Mach 1 over land, where their booms would never be heard on the ground, just the distant rumble of their jet engines. The plane hasn’t been built, and its engine is still in development.

It has been revealed that but Washington isn’t waiting for the data. A June 2025 executive order directed the FAA to repeal its 1973 sonic boom ban over land. In July 2026, the agency proposed a replacement. Civilian jets, both commercial and private, could fly supersonic over U.S. soil as long as their booms register no more than 0.11 pounds per square foot on the ground, about a twentieth of Concorde’s. That’s about 5 Pa, or slightly less than the pressure felt standing next to the speakers at a live concert (6.5 Pa). But airlines, airports, and Europe’s aviation regulator have questioned whether enough evidence supports the number, which the FAA set without the X-59 having flown over a single community.

Even if the boom fades to a thump, the environmental cost doesn’t. Flying faster than sound means fighting far more drag. According to a 2018 analysis by the International Council on Clean Transportation, a upcoming supersonic airliner would “burn five to seven times as much fuel per passenger as a comparable subsonic jet.” Boom Supersonic says Overture will be able to run entirely on sustainable aviation fuel, but airlines, not manufacturers, decide what goes in the tank.

As Popular Science’s Bill Sweetman wrote in 2002, if you can afford a supersonic jet, “you’re not worried about a few lousy tons of fuel.” But everyone below will bear the cost of supersonic jetsetters’ small travel-time benefit in excess noise and climate-warming emissions.

Shurcliff saw this attempt to relax the rules coming. “Once they start flying, they’re going to want to fly them everywhere,” he told The Latest York Times in 1967, warning that over-water routes would be “like a foot in the door.” Fifty-nine years later, thanks to the FAA, the door is swinging open. It’s up to us to decide whether we’re prepared to live with the repercussions or push back as Shurcliff did more than half a century ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that GM Energy and WeaveGrid are launching a vehicle-to-grid (V2G) pilot that will let select Southern California Edison (SCE) customers send electricity from their EV batteries back to the grid. Eligible drivers could get more than $16,000 in help with equipment and installation, and earn money when the grid needs their power.

GM indicates the pilot participants will be its first EV drivers in California to export power from their cars to their homes. Through the California Energy Commission, eligible customers in SCE’s Emergency Load Reduction Program can get up to $8,000 toward a GM Energy V2H system and up to $8,099 toward eligible installation costs, including connecting the system to the grid.

Sources indicate that chevy, GMC, and Cadillac EV drivers can use time-of-use energy management to take advantage of lower rates and may be paid for participating in eligible demand-response events. How much they save or earn depends on their rate strategy, electricity use, and participation.

GM already offers managed charging through 13 utilities, and each program varies by utility.

It has been revealed that an EV battery stores direct current (DC), and your house and the grid use alternating current (AC). GM’s current home backup system uses a wall-mounted inverter to convert the power. With AC bidirectional charging, the car’s onboard inverter does the job. Moving that work into the car could make the equipment on your garage wall simpler and cheaper to install.

Not in CA, but we use solar, time of use, and EVs to minimize our energy costs. We’re not feeding power back to the grid from our cars, but the combo of TOU, solar and EVs does allow us to reduce costs significantly. Solar covers all the expensive peak power, I have the cars start charging early enough to use any extra solar, and the rest is off peak at half cost.

GM is joining CharIN‘s North American AC V2G task force, which is working to align technical standards, equipment certification, and utility approval requirements. In Southern California, the pilot will give GM and its partners a look at how the process works for drivers, from signing up and getting the hardware installed to getting utility approval and sending power back.

  • IT’S A SUBHEAD that means something and at the same time absolutely nothing.
  • Back in 2007, the Los Angeles Times ran something of an informal rule set for the label, which included general principles of straying from fact only if it were to enhance storytelling, but even these guidelines allow for pretty much anything, and the article noted the power of purposeful deceit, like when filmmakers avoided the “realist trap” altogether and nosedived into pure fiction.
  • What makes a ranking of these films so difficult, then, is that there are so many degrees of “based on a true story.” Are we talking about movies that make this claim, or movies that don’t have to make this claim because it’s so obvious, or movies that both don’t make this claim and yet also somehow find themselves in a half-truth historical territory?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IT’S A SUBHEAD that means something and at the same time absolutely nothing. The text appears on screen during trailers and sometimes before the first images of the movie: “based on a true story.” Are there legal criteria for the label? Do producers have guidelines, rules to follow in order to slap the claim onto advertising? Nope. Not that we could find.

Back in 2007, the Los Angeles Times ran something of an informal rule set for the label, which included general principles of straying from fact only if it were to enhance storytelling, but even these guidelines allow for pretty much anything, and the article noted the power of purposeful deceit, like when filmmakers avoided the “realist trap” altogether and nosedived into pure fiction.

What makes a ranking of these films so difficult, then, is that there are so many degrees of “based on a true story.” Are we talking about movies that make this claim, or movies that don’t have to make this claim because it’s so obvious, or movies that both don’t make this claim and yet also somehow find themselves in a half-truth historical territory?

In a recent development, biopics—films about historical persons—are obviously all based on true stories insofar as their primary character did in fact live and eat and poop, at some moment in time. To include these films, however, would make our list almost endless, since Hollywood loves a good biopic, and because there are so many of them. (Sidenote: Hollywood loves anything that reeks of verisimilitude and has been cranking out true-ish stories at a seemingly increasing rate over the last couple decades).

And so our problem: there are too many damn films.

Our solution: no biopics. Also, we’re skewing a bit more modern with our list. We’re also going to be a little snobby. We’re going with a narrow category of “based on a true story.” That is: movies where the creators went further than simply adapting a book or article. These are movies that employ cinematic techniques that make their work stand apart from the original medium. Sometimes, these works question the veracity of the original story. Other times they find totally different ways of telling the same story, making use of all of film’s particular advantages.

According to recent reports, another question we’re asking: Would it be a good movie if it wasn’t true? Zero Dark Thirty, Selma, The Imitation Game, Spotlight, Nomadland, etc. etc. Great true stories put to screen? Yes. Great movies if they were depicting totally fictional events? Ehhhh.

Obviously, there's a lot to choose from. We did our best.

Here are the best movies based on true events.

Industry observers note that let's start with something pretty uncontroversial. At least, in terms of its praise. Based on the life of T. E. Lawrence, the film is epic in every sense of the word, a treat not just for fans of history but for connoisseurs of cinema. Never again will we probably see that level of practical set pieces and horse riding on screen. Based on history, the film itself has become something of its own historical moment.

It has been revealed that roma is the Speak, Memory of cinema: an artfully crafted autobiography that bucks its own conventions. Here, Mexican filmmaker Alfonso Cuarón choses to disregard his own experiences. Instead, the filmmaker focuses on his former live-in housekeeper, a Mixteco woman who held his family together during marriage turmoil. Call it contemporary neorealism or abstract autofiction or whatever. It's a masterpiece.

It has been revealed that the source material for director Adam McKay's finance thriller is Michael Lewis' book of the same name. And the source material for that is, well, the financial crisis. What makes McKay's film so good is tone and form. It veers into meta storytelling without being too heavy-handed. And into humor and comedy without being obnoxiously ironic. It gets the facts right, but it does so in a way that also gets the emotions right.

In a recent development, chronicling the rise of the so-called Golden Age of Porn, Boogie Nights didn't need to do much tonal alteration to make the story sing. Based on the pornstar John Holmes', er, eccentricities, Paul Thomas Anderson's classic somehow both gets to be one of the best movies of the '90s as well as, in some ways, true to life.

Industry observers note that as noted with The Significant Short, it's not just the story itself we talk about when we talk about adaptation. It's the form. Dunkirk could have been a straight-laced chronological retelling of the Battle of Dunkirk. Instead, director Christopher Nolan takes a more ambitious approach: manipulating time and chronology in order to capture the feeling of the fight, how such vital global events came down to small choices—and tiny, almost banal individual heroics.

In a recent development, we should put some "true crime" on this list. (We actually have a whole separate list for this category, but, ya know.) Adapted from reporter Roberto Saviano's insane investigative work of the same name, Gomorrah avoids all cinematic theatrics for a sobering look at Neapolitan crime. If The Godfather is Shakespeare, Gomorrah is Dickens.

Recent findings suggest that if you want a case study in "based on a true story," watch Netflix's 22 July and Norway's Utøya: July 22. Both depict the 2011 mass shooting at the summer camp on Utøya island, which left over 60 children dead. The American version choses a more removed approaching, telling the larger story of the attacks. The Norwegian version choses a kind of subjective impressionism, depicting only the hours of the shooting and filmed in a one-take style. It's probably the most horrifying thing you will ever watch and, we think, a masterclass in historical adaptation.

Sources indicate that another mass shooting movie? Yep. Gus Van Sant's Elephant isn't explicitly about the Columbine school shooting, although the parallels are difficult to ignore. Like Utøya: July 22, the approach is impressionistic, putting viewers inside the school, drifting its cold, unfeeling camera down hallways and into classrooms. No other film has better captured an event that remains, tragically, all too relevant.

In a recent development, cinema has more realism tricks than the found-footage style of the above entries. One, surprisingly, is animation. Unlike live action, animation can visualize abstraction without bending into uncanny CGI; because the style is consistent, artists are able to twist images without readers being pulled out of the work. Based on one soldier's experiences during the 1982 Lebanon War, Waltz With Bashir does exactly this. It probes memory, visualizing trauma and torment like only animation can.

The Diving Bell and the Butterfly (2007).

We're going to keep saying the word "impressionistic" on this list, so we should probably define it. While some artistic styles seek clear verisimilitude—depicting things as they might have seen from without—impressionistic filmmaking is an attempt at phenomenology, capturing what it must be like from within. "From within" best explains The Diving Bell and the Butterfly, which is based on the story of Jean-Dominique Bauby who, at 43, suffered a seizure which caused "locked-in syndrome," meaning, for the rest of his life, he could only see and hear, but not move. The film does its best to capture this from Bauby's perspective. The result is magic.

We haven't really had a straight adaptation on this list yet. So here it is. All the President's Men is based on the book of the same name by reporters Carl Bernstein and Bob Woodward. The result is an equally sobering account of the Watergate political scandal. No style over substance here. Just great dramatization. While there are notable contemporary examples of this approach to "based on a true story," we're going to limit this list to just this one. Sorry, Spotlight.

Right. So we mentioned no biopics. And it's arguable how biopic this biopic biopics. If anything, Nicolas Winding Refn's visualization of one violent inmate's incarceration stands as a great example of successful bombast—totally disregarding a viewer's need of objective clarity and just going full bat-shit impressionism on a story. We appreciate it.

Recent findings suggest that less stylistic than Bronson, but more than All the President's Men, Steve McQueen's 2013 Oscar winner is maybe the perfect iteration of this form. What is real remains real, and what wasn't real but probably could have been real also feels real. Which is to say: We accept everything we see. And we feel it. For another great historical adaptation from McQueen, check out Hunger.

What begins as a seemingly clear adaptation of persons and events evolves into something far more interesting, challenging, and narratively complex. A Beautiful Mind shines as an adapted story because of its trickery, its commitment to its protagonist—not only to his life but his experience of that life.

Sources indicate that as with Waltz With Bashir, studio Ghibli's adaptation (here, a short story about the 1945 firebombing of Kobe) challenges what we expect from "true story" mediums. One might think animation removes readers from the horrors of the events depicted, but it's actually the opposite: somehow, the contrast between the seemingly puerile style of animation and the horror these characters experience makes the film all the move gutting.

In a recent development, why? you ask. Because! Say what you will about the film's melodrama and tear-bating, James Cameron's Titanic just ... works. It's pure historical fiction; nothing in this movie is real besides the ship and the iceberg. Still, Cameron finds a way to make movie magic out of the event. Remember what we noted about diverging from fact in order to serve storytelling? That's exactly what's happening here. These choices work. And they work even better when the audience has some historical footing to stand on.

It may be one of the most straightforward adaptations on this list—in that the film isn't playing too much with form, information, or reality. Still, Spielberg's (best?) film is not simply documentary. The movie finds the director at the height of his storytelling powers, using the story of Oskar Schindler to attempt something much bigger: making sense of modern history's most unfathomable crimes.

Industry observers note that right. So The Wrestler isn't a biopic. Nor is it explicitly based on a true story. Why is it on here? Because Darren Aronofsky's depiction of late-career Randy "The Ram" Robinson (fake) is something like a pastiche of similar real life stories. Aronofsky drew from several in order to craft The Wrestler's central character. Which, in a way, makes the story more real than many realize, even if its mostly false. The parts that are real hit you even harder, like a folding chair to the spine.

In a recent development, A final entry for animation. Mary and Max uses stop motion to tell the story of two real penpals, the Australian filmmaker (Adam Elliot) and a New Yorker living with Asperger syndrome. As with the other animated entries on here, the film makes use of its medium to do what live action can't. In this case, the stop motion form enhances the eccentricities of the characters, while also providing unexpected windows to hit viewers with those #Feels.

In a recent development, if there were any ramifications to the "based on a true story" tagline Hollywood loves so much, then Oliver Stone's JFK would be making attorneys work some long hours. The film is, well, let's just say it's sort of speculative, bordering on conspiratorial. But that's what the story of the JFK assassination is, too. The film doesn't necessarily capture the event so much as the discourse around it, and, in that sense, forges a different kind of accuracy.

Joshua St Clair is an Assistant Editor at Men's Health Magazine.
