Latest Update: High Fat Diet Linked to Higher Colon Cancer Risk, Early Research Demonstrates

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a fresh study, researchers report that a high fat diet may potentially increase the risk of colon cancer.
  • The researchers from Arizona State University noted a diet high in certain fats can cause lasting changes in intestinal stem cells that lead to the development of tumors and the possibility of colon cancer.
  • The study was conducted in mice, but the researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may explain their growth and survival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a fresh study, researchers report that a high fat diet may potentially increase the risk of colon cancer.

The researchers from Arizona State University noted a diet high in certain fats can cause lasting changes in intestinal stem cells that lead to the development of tumors and the possibility of colon cancer.

The study was conducted in mice, but the researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may explain their growth and survival.

The researchers published their findings on November 12 in the journal Stem Cell Reports.

Sources indicate that the researchers stated the study is crucial because 1 in 25 people develop colon cancer in their lifetime. In the United States, that translates into about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer every year. About 55,000 males and 55,000 females are expected to die from the disease in 2026.

Experts not involved in the study say the research provides valuable information, but they have reservations about the results, as the findings do not yet apply to humans.

“The findings provide a potential mechanism linking diet to intestinal cancer development, but we need to be cautious about translating these results to humans,” said Dalia Perelman, MS, CDE, a research dietitian at Stanford University in California.

Recent findings suggest that “We already have evidence from human studies that obesity and certain dietary patterns, particularly those high in processed meats and low in fiber-rich foods, are associated with increased colorectal cancer risk,” Perelman told Healthline. “This study adds a potentially vital mechanism to investigate, but it does not establish that dietary fat itself increases colorectal cancer risk in humans.”.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, shared similar views.

“This study provides a better understanding at the cellular level of how a high fat diet may contribute to colorectal cancer development,” Thanki told Healthline.

“Animal studies are an important starting point for understanding biological processes, but we must be cautious about directly applying their findings to humans,” he added. “Mice and humans share many cellular and biological mechanisms, which makes these studies valuable in identifying potential pathways involved in disease development. However, human diets, genetics, metabolism, and environmental exposures are more complex.”.

To reach their findings, the Arizona State researchers fed mice what the scientists described as a Western-style high fat diet for 6 months.

They then compared those results with those from mice given a low fat diet.

The researchers noted the mice on the high fat diet gained more weight than the mice on the low-fat diet. They also developed more intestinal stem cells, and those cells grew at a more rapid rate.

They added that mice genetically predisposed to intestinal cancer who were fed a high-fat diet developed more and larger tumors.

The researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may help explain their increased growth and survival.

They also pointed out that stem cell behavior returned to normal after high fat diet mice were switched to a low fat diet, although some DNA changes persisted. After four weeks, approximately 18% of these changes remained.

When mice were returned to a high fat diet, the researchers mentioned their intestinal stem cells responded more quickly and strongly than those of mice exposed to the diet for the first time.

They concluded that the study suggests that maintaining a healthy, low fat diet may help regulate intestinal stem cell growth and reduce colon cancer risk.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, RD, president of KAK Consulting and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Ohio, wasn’t involved in the study but highlighted a particular aspect of the findings.

According to recent reports, “What I found particularly interesting was that even after the mice returned to a low fat diet, some of the molecular changes persisted,” she told Healthline. “This raises questions about how our dietary patterns over time may influence long-term health.”.

Experts said these new findings are interesting but noted numerous caveats.

“One key takeaway is that dietary habits over time matter,” stated Thanki. “Even if someone has consumed a high fat diet for years, making changes now may still provide meaningful health benefits.”.

“I also think these findings are particularly vital for children and adolescents, as establishing healthier dietary habits early in life may provide long-term benefits,” he added.

However, Thanki noted that not all fats are the same. “The health risks depend partly on the type of fat consumed, how much is consumed, and what foods make up the overall diet,” he mentioned.

“Diets consistently high in saturated fats, particularly those containing large amounts of processed meats, fried foods, and highly processed products, can contribute to obesity, elevated cholesterol, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction. These factors can also contribute to chronic inflammation and may increase the risk of certain cancers, including colorectal cancer,” Thanki continued.

Perelman noted the diet used in the study was extremely high in fat, providing 60% of calories from fat, primarily from lard.

“We know that the health effects of dietary fats differ depending on their sources and fatty acid composition, and we cannot assume that a diet rich in unsaturated fats from foods such as olive oil, nuts, and seeds would produce the same effects,” she noted.

Perelman added that the researchers primarily studied stem cells from the small intestine rather than the colon.

“Although these tissues share some biological characteristics, they have key differences, and we cannot assume that the same changes would occur in the colon,” she explained.

Finally, Perelman noted that “the mice consuming the high fat diet also gained weight, making it difficult to separate the effects of dietary fat itself from those associated with increased body fat and other metabolic changes.”.

Not all high fat foods are unhealthy. Some high fat foods that offer healthy benefits include:.

“The goal shouldn’t necessarily be to eliminate fat because our bodies need healthy fats for normal functioning,” remarked Thanki. “Instead, people should focus on reducing saturated and trans fats while incorporating healthier unsaturated fats in appropriate amounts.”.

It has been revealed that thanki had several dietary suggestions. Among them:.

Sources indicate that “Consistency matters more than perfection. Even modest dietary changes, maintained over time, can have meaningful health benefits,” Thanki said.

It has been revealed that perelman agreed. “The overall quality of the diet matters. Diets that are very high in fat may displace other foods and nutrients that have important health benefits,” she noted.

“For colorectal cancer specifically, higher intakes of dietary fiber and whole grains have consistently been associated with lower risk,” Perelman noted.

“Therefore, rather than focusing exclusively on reducing fat, it is important to consider the overall dietary pattern and whether it provides adequate amounts of fiber-rich plant foods and other beneficial nutrients.”.

According to recent reports, kirkpatrick agreed that the type of fat is what is important. “A Mediterranean-style diet that includes olive oil, nuts, seeds, and fatty fish can be relatively high in fat but is consistently associated with positive health outcomes,” she said.

“On the other hand, a diet high in saturated fat, processed meats, and ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of certain chronic diseases, particularly when it’s also low in fiber and other protective nutrients.”.

Kirkpatrick also noted that many lifestyle habits contribute to a person’s overall health.

“Our health is influenced by so many factors beyond diet, including how we manage stress, our sleep habits, physical activity, genetics, and overall lifestyle,” she noted.

Spyker's CEO Wants You to ‘Drive the Hell’ Out of His $1.8 Million Supercars

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When people spend nearly $2 million on a two-seat, mid-engine car, you can safely assume it is not the only car in their garage.
  • It has been revealed that but Spyker CEO Victor Muller has a different idea.
  • That's a refreshing philosophy from someone selling a car this pricey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When people spend nearly $2 million on a two-seat, mid-engine car, you can safely assume it is not the only car in their garage. It makes sense that it will not be driven every day; however, often times cars like this are not really driven at all. They spend their entire lives in climate-controlled garages, tucked beneath soft covers. And when the car in question is something like a one-of-25 C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, the temptation to preserve it as a collectible is understandable.

It has been revealed that but Spyker CEO Victor Muller has a different idea. He wants his customers to get behind the wheel and drive. "We prefer to sell our cars to people that actually use them," Muller told me during an interview at Retromobile New York. "Because that's what I made them for. To drive the hell out of them.".

That's a refreshing philosophy from someone selling a car this pricey. Particularly when that car is the new C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, which looks as much like a piece of fine jewelry as an 800-horsepower road rocket. Unfortunately, Muller admits that many of Spyker's previous creations haven't enjoyed particularly active lives.

"Many of our cars, of the 252 we made so far, have just ended up in dungeons, in vaults, in spaces where nobody will ever see them," Muller stated. He's hoping to change that by organizing more owner events and encouraging customers to spend time enjoying their cars; Spyker has joined the Supercar Owners Circle, a global network of car collectors, and is planning gatherings in Europe and the United States.

The organization is also in a position where it can be selective about who gets its cars. According to Muller, all 25 Preliator XXV Coupés sold during their debut at The Quail, a Motorsports Gathering in August. Every single one was snapped up in a day. "I've never seen anything like that in my entire life," he said. Spyker aims to build 25 Spyders and 25 Sedancas in 2028, he added, once production of the Coupés is complete next year.

Who is buying these cars has changed dramatically over the last quarter century. "In 2000, my typical customer was a fifty-five to sixty-year-old industrialist—old money, car collector, very astute buyer," Muller explained. "Fast forward twenty five years. Your average age is thirty-five years. Tech investor. Huge collection. Knows his cars completely. But nobody asks how much it is.".

According to recent reports, muller says approximately 40 percent of his latest buyers are existing or former Spyker owners, and roughly 80 percent of the new cars are expected to go to the United States. But no matter how old the buyer is or where they live, Muller wants them to drive the cars. This makes sense when you understand his approach to engineering; The new car has no massive infotainment screens or hybrid systems, and electronic intervention is largely limited to essential safety features like ABS and stability control.

“If you mis-shift in a Spyker and you drive two hundred miles an hour and you shift to second gear, you blow up the engine," Muller stated. "And I think it has to be that way in Spyker world." For Spyker, the connection between driver and machine is more important than chasing lap records, acceleration figures and electronic nannies. "If you don't like that, buy something else," he added. "If not, man up—drive a Spyker.".

Another way to demonstrate that these cars are meant to be driven is to get the brand back into racing. Muller revealed that Spyker is taking steps toward returning to professional endurance competition. The firm competed in the 24 Hours of Le Mans eight times, most recently in 2010. Naturally, I asked whether another trip to Le Mans might be in Spyker's future.

"Absolutely," Muller noted. "We'd love to go back in racing." Muller states Spyker is preparing to re-enter endurance racing, although he stopped short of announcing a timeline, championship, or confirmed race entry. He certainly likes the idea of seeing his latest creation on the track. More importantly, he's already started putting people in place to make it happen.

"I actually hired my former GT2 race director again," Muller noted. "He started a week ago today.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the last time Hyundai confirmed a latest work truck was 22 years ago, and the Hyundai Porter has proven itself as a dependable workhorse throughout Korea and Southeast Asia – but only the pyramids and the Chevy Express can last forever. Hyundai is reportedly getting ready to pull the wraps off an all-new Porter pickup. This time, it’s electric.

Distinct from the Piaggio-branded Porter pickup that’s already sold in Europe, the Hyundai Porter is a conceptually similar, work-focused vehicle with a dropside pickup “bed” trailing a box-like passenger cab and a serious, professional-grade payload capacity.

Sources indicate that carscoops recently published photos of a heavily camouflaged Hyundai Porter prototype last month, along with claims that Hyundai means to follow up the success of sister brand Kia’s multifunctional PV5 electric vans with a globally available electric version of the truck as early as next year. This week, the wraps came off, giving us our best look yet at what the truck might look like when it makes its official debut.

After feeding as many spy shots as I could into some AI models, we ended up with the images you see here. If they’re accurate, they show a commercial-ready EV that’s meant to attract upcoming fleet buyers looking to ditch diesel in Western markets while serving as a direct, 1:1 replacement for domestic fleet operators already putting Porter pickups to work.

Those operators will probably feel a little safer behind the wheel of the new truck, too. Hyundai has worked a short hood and crash structure into the bodywork where a conventional “flat” cabover now sits – a move that seems to point both to a commitment to provide better front-end protection to the truck’s occupants and an intent to at least take an honest run at the Euro NCAP crash standards.

Beyond that, we don’t really know anything about the upcoming Korean pickup – but it’s a safe bet that the next-generation Porter will benefit from some of the technology that’s been baked into the Hyundai Motor Group’s E-GMP.S commercial vehicle platform that underpins the Kia PV vehicles. Those ship with 51.5 and 71.2 kWh battery options sending electrons to 120 kW (~160 hp) electric motors, and while that’s far from a guarantee, it’s not nothing, either.

Sources indicate that that’s my take, anyway – what’s yours? Will the Hyundai Porter EV make its way to the West on an AWD version of the E-GMP.S platform, or will it remain a regional model running on one of the tech giant’s hybrid platforms? Let us know in the comments.

This is how EV trucks should look, like this and Telo. Stick storage space under the bed like the T2 Transporter.

  • Well, here’s something to melt your face right off: the secret prototype M7 BMW never made.
  • Rated at the same 400 horsepower as the later M5 would have, this car was only just revealed by BMW’s Classic division.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the end of Raiders of the Lost Ark, a nameless government employee wheels the crated-up Ark of the Covenant into a vast and anonymous warehouse, forever to be lost again. You have to imagine this is like what going to work in BMW’s mechanical archives is like, where hidden wonders wait patiently to see the light of day again.

Well, here’s something to melt your face right off: the secret prototype M7 BMW never made. Powered by the 4.9-liter V-8 that would go on to make the E39 M5 such a legend, it's a manual-transmission 1997 short-wheelbase E38 7-series, a total wolf in sheep’s clothing.

Rated at the same 400 horsepower as the later M5 would have, this car was only just revealed by BMW’s Classic division. As a prototype, it’s quite the what-might-have-been story, although BMW probably wasn’t all that serious about producing a full M version of its luxury flagship. Instead, the V-12-powered 750iL that Pierce Brosnan pilots remotely from the back seat in 1997's Tomorrow Never Dies provided plenty of drama.

See all results for BMW 7-series for sale near 03046.

In a recent development, however, the idea of a roomy limousine-class sedan with M5 power certainly gets the imagination going. BMW financed a series of films in the early 2000s featuring Clive Owen as a nameless driver, collected together as The Hire, and the one Guy Ritchie directed featured Owen ferrying Madonna around at breakneck speed in an M5. This M7 prototype would have worked just as well.

Besides the powertrain, a big part of this prototype’s appeal is just how understated it is. BMW’s M division doesn’t really do subtlety much anymore—customers want their carbon-fiber accents and M badges—but this black sedan would have flown completely under the radar in 1997. Engineers out testing it on the unrestricted autobahns must have had a heck of a time.

Sadly, like the E31-chassis, V-12-powered M8 prototype, the M7 would never make its way to a production version. Perhaps, though, that makes it all the more appealing, a secret treasure that’s been kept out of view, now finally breaking cover again. Dr. Jones might argue that it belongs in a museum. We’d sure like to slide behind the wheel and see if this one-off M7 will hit its stated top speed of 155 mph.

Fancy axes and simple pottery show how interconnected Europe was 5,000 years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe.
  • Sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE.
  • “The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals latest insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe. This physical and cultural separation seems to have existed for a very long time. Archaeological evidence on either side of the river as early as the late fourth millennia BCE reveals differences. Archaeologists have determined that the river is a sort of barrier during this time—but upcoming research challenges this conclusion.

Sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. His findings, described in a study recently published in the archaeological journal Germania, suggest that populations in Western, Central, and Northern Europe were more connected than previously assumed.

“The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals latest insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich said in a statement.

Sources indicate that the pottery in question, called coarse ware, is simple and plain—so much so that archaeologists have seen it as culturally insignificant. The roughly-shaped artifacts have emerged in many regions of Europe. It became widespread in modern-day central and northern France as well as the western Alpine region starting in the mid-4th millennium BCE. Afterward, it also became prominent in modern-day western and northern Germany and Denmark.

Industry observers note that “There are indications that a convergence of pottery styles across such great distances occurred gradually and unconsciously. This is an indicator of high mobility within a region where there were no distinct barriers between groups, or where the boundaries were fluid,” remarked Schultrich.

Double stone axes—prestigious axes with two cutting edges and a shaft hole—were also widespread in this period. Archaeologists have discovered them from France through Central Europe to Scandinavia and Poland. While the dates of the French double stone axes has been a subject of contention, it’s currently clear that they, along with the Central and Northern European versions, hail from the the 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. Unlike coarse ware, the double axe design seems to have been intentionally widespread, showing that a shared concept existed on either side of the river.

Industry observers note that the same regions are also home to different versions of large-scale group burials, including passage graves or gallery graves. But they all were the final resting place of dozens to hundreds of individuals, were used over many generations, and were the locations of ritual acts and gatherings. This is more evidence of a shared idea, even though its regional manifestation differed.

“It was not a uniform cultural complex,” Schultrich explained. “What we see here is a network characterised by fundamental narratives, yet one that simultaneously allowed scope for strong regional peculiarities. This is an early example of a complex, differentiated form of society in which identity combined both supra-regional and local elements.”.

By drawing prehistoric connections across the Rhine, Schultrich revealed ties across late Neolithic Europe that clearly overcame the watery boundary.

#145222. Is Conspiracy Thinking in the Person or the Place?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1324 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Is Conspiracy Thinking in the Person or the Place?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that here are three statements.
  • Food should be chosen based on each person's blood group.
  • Evidence of alien contact is being concealed from the public.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Sources indicate that here are three statements. How much do you agree with each?

Food should be chosen based on each person's blood group.

Evidence of alien contact is being concealed from the public.

These seem to have little in common, but people who agree with one tend to agree with the others (Lobato and colleagues, 2014).

All three statements come from questionnaires that measure what researchers call epistemically suspect beliefs: confident claims about how the world works that go beyond, or against, the available evidence.

According to recent reports, because these beliefs hang together so well, many researchers treat them as something close to a personality trait, a stable way of seeing things. Others see them as a response to the world. Conspiracy theories, for example, tend to spread during periods of social crisis (van Prooijen and Douglas, 2017).

Recent findings suggest that if these beliefs are traits, they should stay roughly the same from year to year, regardless of what happens around a person. A response to the world would instead rise and fall as people’s view of that world changes. Most studies cannot tell which is true, because they measure people only once.

Sources indicate that in a paper just published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, my colleagues and I tested the two views (Alper and colleagues, 2026). The project, led by Sinan Alper of Yaşar University. was funded by TÜBİTAK, Türkiye's national science agency.

We surveyed the same adults in Türkiye and the United Kingdom five times, once every six months. At the start, 2,077 people participated in Türkiye and 959 in the UK. Each time, they reported these beliefs and rated corruption among public officials, business executives, and the media, as well as other attitudes.

The two countries differ sharply on corruption. On Transparency International’s (2026) Corruption Perceptions Index, the UK ranks 20th of 182 countries, and Türkiye ranks 124th.

The three beliefs moved together.

Sources indicate that on average, the beliefs declined slightly over the two years, except for conspiracy belief in Türkiye, which revealed no clear change. I wouldn't read much into this, since answering the same questions repeatedly can itself lower scores. What struck me more was how tightly linked the three beliefs were. At the start, the correlations between them were strong, ranging from .65 to .86. Change was linked even more tightly. When a person’s belief in the paranormal fell, their belief in pseudoscience and conspiracy theories tended to fall with it.

It has been revealed that one possibility is that all three reflect a single underlying tendency. Simpler explanations, such as people answering the survey less carefully over time, cannot yet be ruled out. Either way, much of the change is shared, but not all of it.

According to recent reports, in Türkiye, people who saw more corruption over the past two years also became more open to conspiracy theories. Their paranormal and pseudoscientific beliefs did not follow. In the UK, we found no such link.

This may seem to clash with the previous section, and in part it does. Most of the change in these beliefs is shared, but each may keep some room to move on its own. In Türkiye, corruption may have tracked the portion attributable to conspiracy beliefs alone. It makes sense that belief in conspiracy was the one to move. A conspiracy theory claims that powerful people are secretly working together for their own gain. Corruption is often a true version of that story. Black cats and blood-type diets have nothing to do with it.

Sources indicate that at the start of the study, though, the link between perceived corruption and conspiracy belief was about twice as strong in the UK (r = .61) as in Türkiye (r = .32). The difference may come down to how common corruption is. Where it is relatively rare, seeing it everywhere may say more about the person than about the country and may function as a stable trait. Where corruption is widespread and changing, people’s sense of it may follow those changes, and conspiracy beliefs may shift accordingly.

Our answer is both. These beliefs are steady and hang together, but they can still change.

Some factors seem to set a person’s starting point. People higher in authoritarianism, who value discipline and following leaders in unity, endorsed all three kinds of beliefs more in both countries. But changes in authoritarianism did not track changes in belief. Perceived corruption works differently, and whether it moves these beliefs seems to depend on where you live.

It has been revealed that this fits earlier work. Conspiracy beliefs are more common in countries with widespread corruption and in less stable societies, where education offers less protection against them (Alper, 2023). In another study I coauthored, education was also less tied to trust in science in highly corrupt countries (Alper and colleagues, 2024). In such places, people might learn to distrust authority from experience.

When someone you know shares a conspiracy theory, ask two questions. Is this how they see everything, from health advice to the evening news? Or is it a response to something they have watched go wrong? The first kind of belief tends to change slowly. The second should be taken seriously, because sometimes suspicion points at something real.

According to recent reports, careful thinking still matters. In a recent experiment, my colleagues and I found that training designed to encourage reflection lowered conspiracy beliefs (Bayrak and colleagues, 2025). But when institutions keep giving people reasons to be suspicious, better thinking can only do so much. I guess that in some places the best answer to conspiracy thinking is institutions that give people less to suspect. Survey data like ours cannot settle that.

It has been revealed that sinan Alper and I have begun to test it experimentally. In two preregistered studies with nationally representative US samples, we described an unnamed US state or a fictional country as either highly corrupt or very clean (Alper and Yilmaz, 2026).

According to recent reports, people found conspiracy claims about the corrupt place far more believable, and this was most closely tied to a sense that resources were being shared unfairly. The paper is still under peer review, and I will write about it once it is done.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Developed by Japanese material handling giant Tadano, the 35-ton V320RC wheeled electric pick & carry crane has spent the last few months proving itself at NMG Italia’s job sites, where it’s been handling heavy loads in tight industrial spaces and improving efficiency by 50%.
  • Developed in collaboration with NMG Italia, the V320RC electric crane has already proven its performance in the field with NMG and during precision setup operations at Marmomac, a trade show dedicated to the marble industry held each year in Verona.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Developed by Japanese material handling giant Tadano, the 35-ton V320RC wheeled electric pick & carry crane has spent the last few months proving itself at NMG Italia’s job sites, where it’s been handling heavy loads in tight industrial spaces and improving efficiency by 50%. And now, you can buy one.

Developed in collaboration with NMG Italia, the V320RC electric crane has already proven its performance in the field with NMG and during precision setup operations at Marmomac, a trade show dedicated to the marble industry held each year in Verona.

In a recent development, “The (Tadano) V320RC marks a real breakthrough in the pick & carry industry,” reads the official Tadano launch copy. “Rather than an evolution of existing solutions, it introduces a new philosophy, with technologies and features capable of setting new benchmarks in the lifting market. Tadano and NMG Italia continue their collaboration in the field, turning real-world experience into new technological solutions to meet the most advanced demands of industrial lifting.”.

The crane itself is a compact, battery-electric pick-and-carry machine with a maximum lifting capacity of 35 tonnes. Measuring just 5 m long, 2.15 m wide and 2.400 m tall (a meter is about a yard, guys – you got this), the V320RC is designed to bring heavy lifting capability into tight industrial spaces where larger cranes struggle to operate.

The upcoming Tadano runs on a 120V, 1,120 Ah li-ion battery pack (that works out to ~134 kWh) and packs a gross vehicle weight of more than 31,150 kg (~34.5 short tones). That number includes 9,500 kg (~10 tons) of removable counterweights that make transport and handling easier for a wider range of customers. Under the hood, a new hydraulic system pairs a variable-displacement pump with what the tech giant calls “an electro-hydraulic control valve” to improve precision and responsiveness while reducing energy consumption.

According to NMG Italia, all that baked-in tech V320RC give them 50% better productivity than competing electric cranes working under equivalent workloads, with enough battery capacity to support several days of operation between charges.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If the Fast & Furious franchise taught us anything, it’s that there’s always another gear, and there’s no such thing as a bad plot­line. (Also: family.) To honor its silver anniversary, here’s a recap of the F&F universe, as it expanded from the L.A. street-racing scene to encompass every action-film trope, device, and format ever scrawled on a Hollywood studio whiteboard.

The Fast and the Furious (2001).

Cop Brian O’Connor infiltrates the L.A. import-car scene to bust hijackers who steal DVD players and at least one sweet 13-inch TV/VCR combo. He bonds with bald kingpin Dominic Toretto, then lets him go. Executives smell a sequel. Toretto has other aims: The Chronicles of Riddick. Danger to manifold: 10/10.

Now a fugitive with a Nissan Skyline but no visible means of support, Brian joins the feds to catch a drug lord who tortures a corrupt cop with the ol’ rat-in-the-ice-bucket trick. Roman Pearce replaces Dom as the bald guy at the emotional core. Camaro jumps onto yacht. Danger to manifold: 5/10.

The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift (2006).

The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift (2006).

Recent findings suggest that brian who? Now it’s Sean, a high schooler who looks like he’s 35. Busted for street racing, he’s sent to Tokyo, the capital of street racing. He crosses the yakuza-­connected Drift King and falls in with Han Seoul-­Oh, who can’t stop snacking. Dom cameo as sequel bait. Danger to manifold: 七/10.

Recent findings suggest that dom’s back, and the crew now executes road-train robberies in the Dominican Republic. Brian, now FBI, infiltrates a heroin pipeline. Letty dies. Dom seeks vengeance. A Road Warrior–style chase ends in a killer wheelie, literally. Dom is busted, but a sequel is nigh. Danger to manifold: 3/10.

Street racing? Nah. We’re a heist franchise, dog. Dom’s crew, now fully Hollywood four-quadrant tested, steals a crime lord’s fortune in Brazil. A former wrestler shows up as DSS agent Luke Hobbs. Bald jokes and legal ambiguity ensue. Everybody walks with $100 million. Danger to manifold: 1.5/10.

Hobbs is back, and we meet British scoundrel number one, Owen Shaw, an ex-SAS mercenary who drives a ramp car that flips police cruisers like a spatula. Letty is alive (huh?), with amnesia, and on Shaw’s payroll. Gisele dies. (Who’s Gisele again?) Danger to manifold: –10/10.

According to recent reports, jason Statham (really?) is Deckard Shaw, Owen’s scoundrel brother, who fireballs Dom’s family home. The crew parachutes into Azerbaijan in their cars. A Lykan HyperSport jumps between three Abu Dhabi office towers. Han’s dead (like we believe that). The saddest ending imaginable. Danger to manifold: N/A.

Fate, F9, Fast X, Hobbs & Shaw (2017–23).

Recent findings suggest that roll call: John Cena. Dame Helen Mirren. Charlize Theron. Jason Momoa. Sir Idris Elba. Old villains are in the crew now. We’re in Cuba (thanks, Obama), Antarctica, a sub­marine, and a Pontiac Fiero in space. Han? Gisele? Both alive. It’s just a parody of action movies now, right? Danger to manifold: $7 billion/10.

Albatross couple George and Geraldine lay an egg

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A bird couple with a long history has laid their first (and likely only) egg of the 2026-2027 season.
  • According to Friends of Midway Atoll, the pair did not produce an egg last year, making this arrival “especially exciting news.”.
  • Recent findings suggest that short-tailed albatrosses are almost completely white and have a large pink bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A bird couple with a long history has laid their first (and likely only) egg of the 2026-2027 season. United States Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) volunteer and photographer Dan Rapp spotted the egg on George and Geraldine’s nest this weekend. The pair are endangered short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian, and this is their 10th straight year together.

According to Friends of Midway Atoll, the pair did not produce an egg last year, making this arrival “especially exciting news.”.

Recent findings suggest that short-tailed albatrosses are almost completely white and have a large pink bill. The monogamous birds can live up to 50 years, and nest on islands and atolls where they typically lay one egg per season. Short-tailed albatrosses are listed as endangered, and biologists estimate that there are only 10,000 left in the wild.

It has been revealed that george and Geraldine were banded as chicks on Torishima Island, Japan. They raised their first chick together during the 2018–2019 breeding season. The duo is the only breeding pair of short-tailed albatross on the Midway Atoll, but other members of their species were observed last season. After spending the summer/non-nesting season apart, George was first spotted at Midway Atoll on October 18. He was reunited with Geraldine by October 22.

This remote group of islands sit about 1,250 miles from Hawaii’s capital Honolulu and are most famous for a pivotal World War II battle. Every fall, it becomes a temporary home to the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species. Some notable albatross species are the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species and the Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis). At over 70 years old, a Laysan albatross named Wisdom claims the title of oldest known banded wild bird. She has produced roughly 50 to 60 eggs, and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime, and she became a grandmother once again in March. Wisdom has not been spotted yet this nesting season.

According to recent reports, bird enthusiasts from around the world can eavesdrop on this albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates. Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch fluffy albatross chicks.

#145218. Tech Report: How Kelly Rowland Keeps Her Eczema Flare-Ups Under Control During Winter

Tech Report: How Kelly Rowland Keeps Her Eczema Flare-Ups Under Control During Winter

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that wintertime can bring everyone down with its colder weather and less sunlight.
  • Sources indicate that that’s the case for Grammy-winning singer, actress, and Destiny’s Child alum Kelly Rowland, who has been living with eczema since her 20s.
  • “[You] don’t know what the environment is going to give you—because mine is also environmental—or what the weather is going to give you,” Rowland told Healthline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that wintertime can bring everyone down with its colder weather and less sunlight. But for those with eczema, this time of year can wreak havoc on their skin, too.

Sources indicate that that’s the case for Grammy-winning singer, actress, and Destiny’s Child alum Kelly Rowland, who has been living with eczema since her 20s. During the winter months, she often dreads the cold.

“[You] don’t know what the environment is going to give you—because mine is also environmental—or what the weather is going to give you,” Rowland told Healthline.

Cold weather and indoor heating can reduce humidity, drying out the skin and triggering or worsening eczema flare-ups.

“[What we know] about the skin barrier is that it really is like a gate or wall against the outside world,” Camille Howard-Verovic, MD, a dermatologist at Active Dermatology, told Healthline.

In healthy skin, the barrier controls what enters and leaves the skin. However, for people with eczema, Howard-Verovic noted they have skin barrier dysfunction, which allows substances such as allergens and irritants to penetrate the skin.

Cold weather can increase transepidermal water loss, a process in which moisture escapes through the skin’s outer barrier and evaporates into the surrounding air.

It has been revealed that “People with eczema have a tremendous amount of transepidermal water loss, so you’re just drier,” stated Howard-Verovic. “[You’re] not holding onto the water as well, so that causes the itching and the rash that we feel when we have eczema.”.

Rowland first noticed eczema flares behind her ears as well as on her elbows, arms, and the back of her knees.

“[It] looked like a rash, so that’s what I thought it was all this time, and I dealt with it for so long until after I had my son and then it started to get worse on my face,” she noted.

She eventually went to a dermatologist who diagnosed her with moderate-to-severe eczema, a chronic inflammatory skin condition that can cause intense itching, painful skin cracking, thickened skin, and redness or swelling.

When Rowland learned that eczema can be genetic, it made sense to her.

“I remember seeing big rashes on [my mom’s] neck and her arms…so she had it, and I guess I was the lucky one,” stated Rowland.

At first, she tried eliminating foods that she thought might be triggers. She also bathed in oatmeal.

“[I] literally have had a tub full of oatmeal, like literally went to the store to get store-bought fresh oats,” she said. “I tried everything, and it doesn’t help until you go talk to a doctor about it.”.

At first, she tried prescription topical medications but found them cumbersome.

“I don’t have the time, if I’m being honest, and we live in a world that is moving so fast…I started buying like three tubes of whatever it was I was using and losing it; it was just too much for me,” Rowland said.

It has been revealed that rowland said she found relief with Ebglyss, a prescription injectable medication for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. She has also partnered with Eli Lilly and Company, its manufacturer, to raise awareness about eczema.

Rowland remarked she’s sharing her experience to help others living with eczema, including people she’s met who have experienced greater challenges managing the condition.

“One lady was telling me about how she’s having a tough time [looking] in the mirror cause she doesn’t know who’s looking back at her, and she saw her skin before eczema and after,” noted Rowland.

When she first had symptoms, she said she felt embarrassed, too.

“[Because] it was just in the middle of my arm space and…[if I] put out my hand to shake someone’s hand, you don’t know if somebody’s judgy,” she remarked.

Rowland hopes being open about her condition will encourage others to advocate for themselves and talk with their doctor about treatment options.

Because eczema can look different on deeper skin tones, Howard-Verovic noted that a dermatologist can help make the correct diagnosis.

“Some people may not even know that they have eczema,” she said. “We know that eczema is a rash; it can appear red on certain skin tones, and it can be grey or white on certain skin tones, so it can look a little different.”.

In addition to medication, Rowland said managing stress helps reduce her eczema flare-ups.

It has been revealed that “Before [when] I went on tour, because I was under so much stress, it flared up like crazy, like you wouldn’t believe,” she said. “We were in the back trying to figure out how to cover certain things up, and we figured some of it out, and some of it was really tricky, but what helped was when I actually just calmed down…not that it helped overnight, but it did just kind of bring the flare down.”.

She stated red light therapy, feeling grounded outside without her shoes on, getting vitamin D from natural sunlight, and cooking are ways she reduces ongoing stress.

Sources indicate that “Cooking calms me when my kids aren’t here, and I have a really good [Zen] playlist on,” stated Rowland. “[If] you ask me a question [in those moments], I might give you my heart; I’m just so happy.”.

She also tries to cut back on sugar, which she believes triggers flares.

Another way to reduce flares, according to Howard-Verovic, is to avoid hot showers, especially in the winter.

“[We] know eczematous skin likes lukewarm water,” she noted.

Because Howard-Verovic and her daughter both live with eczema, she set a rule about when it’s time to get out of the shower.

It has been revealed that “[If] you see condensation on the bathroom mirror, you’ve spent too much time in the shower,” mentioned Howard-Verovic. “[That] really hot, hot water feels really good in that moment…but when you get out all that water evaporates, and there’s no moisture in the atmosphere, and it dries your skin out, and now your skin is unhappy again.”.

If you prefer to take baths, she remarked use gentle cleansers.

“[There] are bleach baths for really, really bad flare-ups,” she noted.

Diluted bleach baths are sometimes recommended for people with eczema, but they should only be used according to a healthcare professional’s instructions.

As soon as you get out of the shower or bath, Howard-Verovic stated to apply a quality moisturizer to your damp skin. According to the National Eczema Association (NEA), lotions containing the following ingredients can help ease dry skin associated with eczema.

To help identify appropriate products, look for ones that have the NEA’s Seal of Acceptance.
